newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Little Taiwan fanfare for Madame Chiang at 100.
newsitem.headline: Little Taiwan fanfare for Madame Chiang at 100.

text.p: Taiwan on Wednesday was making no special preparations to mark the 100th birthday of Madame Chiang Kai-shek, widow of the once-feared Chinese generalissimo whose image has fallen hard in recent years.

Madame Chiang, who with her husband held supreme status in China until 1949 and later in exile in Taiwan, was greeted on Wednesday at her New York City home by elders of Taiwan's ruling Nationalist Party.

But Taiwan's current Nationalist powers-that-be took little heed at home, reflecting the party's metamorphosis into a local-minded political machine that has long since abandoned the Chiangs' fading dream of "retaking the Chinese mainland".
Taiwan television showed an alert and elegantly dressed Madame Chiang cheerfully greeting a government delegation amid 100 red roses sent by President Lee Teng-hui.
"That's a lovely, lovely painting. It's unique," the centenarian, poised as ever in cheongsam and jade earrings, said in English as she received a Chinese watercolour scroll.

The delegation included party vice chairman Yu Kuo-hwa and senior presidential adviser Shen Chang-hun, both 83 years old and rarely heard in modern Taiwan's rough-and-tumble democratic political jostle.

Madame Chiang, who captivated the American public during World War Two and appealed passionately to the U.S. Congress for help against the occupying Japanese, turns 100 on Thursday as under the Chinese lunar calendar.
Elderly Chinese typically celebrate their birthdays and other significant events based on the lunar calendar, meaning the dates change from year to year on the gregorian calendar.
Chiang Kai-shek and his Republic of China government fled into exile on Taiwan in 1949 after his Nationalist troops lost a civil war on the mainland to Mao Zedong's communist army.
For four decades, Chiang ruled Taiwan with an authoritarian fist, with Madame Chiang often putting a softer face on the exiled government and its claim of sovereignty over China.
Madame Chiang, born Soong May-ling in Guangdong province in 1897, moved to New York's Long Island after her husband's death in 1975 and has largely withdrawn from the public eye.
The Chiang family's power -- and its patriarch's icon status -- began to fade in Taiwan in 1988 with the death of President Chiang Ching-kuo, Chiang Kai-shek's son from a previous marriage.
Taipei recently erected a monument bearing an inscription holding Chiang Kai-shek responsible for ordering troops who slaughtered thousands of Taiwanese in a 1947 massacre.
